exp_design: Based on aerial photographs from 1996 (and in some cases 1984–1985) we selected all forest patches of more than 1 km2. Of these (approximately 40), we selected 15 areas evenly distributed in the elevational range of 1700–2000 m asl. In a similar manner we selected all agricultural areas of more than 1 km2 from aerial photos from 1967, 1975, and 1984–1985. To be considered an agricultural site, the area had to have been in cultivation on the oldest available aerial photo. On the basis of this initial selection we selected 15 sites that were evenly distributed in the area and in the same elevational range as the forest sites. Finally, we selected all stands (around 20) that appeared to be exotic tree plantations (i.e., dense tree cover in an area that in the oldest aerial photos was treeless). In the field we randomly selected one tree in each of the forest sites in an area that was minimally disturbed by humans (selective logging, beehives, coffee production) and >200 m from the forest edge. In the center of the agricultural sites, we selected a mature shade tree in a home garden with coffee (in one site we found no such home garden, hence n = 14). In the plantations we selected a random tree in the middle of the stand. We selected 7 Cupressus-plantations and six Eucalyptus plantations (n = 13 exotic plantations) to get an even distribution between the two plantation types. (See Supporting Information for a list of the sites and Fig. 1 for the distribution of the sites across the investigated landscape.)

C_out_exp_design: Bean plants were sampled on six occasions: 17 April (1 wk after emergence), 25 April, 3 May, 12 May, 19 May, and 17 June. The sample unit on 17 April, 25 April, 3 May, and 19 May (samples 1Ð3 and 5) was a 3.35-cm2 disc removed with a cork borer from upper and lower stratum leaves (McAuslane et al. 1995). The disc was removed from the underside of the central leaßet to the right of the mid-vein. Five plants per plot were sampled on these dates. The average of the two discs was used in treatment analysis. On 12 May and 17 June (samples 4 and 6), one whole plant per subplot replicate was sampled.

title: Different crop rotation systems as drivers of change in soil bacterial community structure and yield of rice, Oryza sativa
exp_design: The experiment was set-up as a randomized block design with four treatments and four replicates of each treatment. Rice was rotated with maize and mungbean in different combinations. Each year, the three cropping periods were November–February (only rice crop in all treatments), March–June (rotation crops) and July–October (rice or maize crops) with four treatments: (1) rice–rice–rice (RRR) as control, (2) rice–maize–rice (RMR), (3) rice–mungbeanmaize (RMgM), and (4) rice–mungbean–rice (RMgR). These crop rotation treatments were repeated yearly from 2001 to 2008.

title: Intercropping with fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) enhanced seed yield and reduced Orobanche foetida infestation in faba bean (Vicia faba)
exp_design: In the two cropping seasons of 2007–2008 and 2008–2009, the two faba bean genotypes were grown as a mono-crop (25 plants per m2) or inter-cropped in the same row with fenugreek (local landrace from Beja region, Tunisia) at plant densities (25 plants of faba bean and 40 fenugreek plants per m2) in a field naturally infested with O. foetida. In both seasons, the trial was implemented in different parts of the same field. The experimental design was a randomized complete block with four replications. Each genotype was sown in 4 rows, 4 m long, with 0.5 m inter-row spacing.

exp_design: Each experiment had 13 treatments arrangement with 3 replications in a randomized complete block design. Each plot size was 6 × 3 m.
time_raw: Experiments were conducted during the rainy seasons of two consecutive years (2003 and 2004). Baby corn (Zea mays L. cv. VL-16), soybean (Glycine max cv. Alankar), green gram (Phaseolus aureus Roxb. cv. B-105), black gram (Vigna mungo Roxb. cv. T-9), and groundnut (Arachis hypogea cv. GG-2) were sown on June 18, 2003 and June 24, 2004. Baby corn was harvested on September 8, 2003 and September 11, 2004, whereas Green gram and black gram were harvested on September 15, 2003 and September 29, 2004. Soybean and groundnut were harvested on October 4, 2003 and October 15, 2004.

T_subpractice_description_raw: One row of soybean sown at 30 cm spacing in between of two rows of baby corn

T_tillage_subpractice_raw: power tiller ploughing followed by harrowing
T_intercrop_subpractice: Intercrop (N fixing and Non N fixing)
C_fert_subpractice_raw: The fertilizer schedule was 150:100:100 kg N, P2O5 and K2O ha−1 for monocropped and intercropped baby corn and 40:60:60 (N, P2O5, K2O) for monocropped legumes. Half of the N was applied through vermicompost (1.5–0.65–1.2) in baby corn as basal application. Proportionate fertilizers were also applied to intercropped legumes along the rows. One-fourth of nitrogen in the form of urea (46–0–0) and the whole amount of P2O5 and K2O in the form of single super phosphate (0–16–0) and muriate of potash (0–0–60) respectively were applied as basal and remaining one-fourth nitrogen was top dressed at 30 days after sowing (DAS). The total amount of N, P2O5, and K2O in the form of urea, SSP, and MOP was applied as basal in legumes.

exp_design: Each experiment had 13 treatments arrangement with 3 replications in a randomized complete block design. Each plot size was 6 × 3 m.
time_raw: Experiments were conducted during the rainy seasons of two consecutive years (2003 and 2004). Baby corn (Zea mays L. cv. VL-16), soybean (Glycine max cv. Alankar), green gram (Phaseolus aureus Roxb. cv. B-105), black gram (Vigna mungo Roxb. cv. T-9), and groundnut (Arachis hypogea cv. GG-2) were sown on June 18, 2003 and June 24, 2004. Baby corn was harvested on September 8, 2003 and September 11, 2004, whereas Green gram and black gram were harvested on September 15, 2003 and September 29, 2004. Soybean and groundnut were harvested on October 4, 2003 and October 15, 2004.
C_subpractice_description_raw: Baby corn sown at 60 cm spacing as monocrop
T_subpractice_description_raw: One row of groundnut sown at 30 cm spacing in between of two rows of baby corn
C_tillage_subpractice_raw: power tiller ploughing followed by harrowing
T_tillage_subpractice_raw: power tiller ploughing followed by harrowing
T_intercrop_subpractice: Intercrop (N fixing and Non N fixing)
C_fert_subpractice_raw: The fertilizer schedule was 150:100:100 kg N, P2O5 and K2O ha−1 for monocropped and intercropped baby corn and 40:60:60 (N, P2O5, K2O) for monocropped legumes. Half of the N was applied through vermicompost (1.5–0.65–1.2) in baby corn as basal application. Proportionate fertilizers were also applied to intercropped legumes along the rows.
